items.title: Minor "Ram" Hall Interview, 1958-09-02
items.q: I said old man Contra, taught me how to, he said all the way to let your drum down unless the weather gets too tight.

ctx.x: I think you said he was. Sure. Yeah, tune them up. One of them to B and one to A or one to E or something. A certain pitch.

Like I said about the studio drummer, I told him what to do and he came back the next week and said, it's fine now. Yeah. He loved the way I told him. I said old man Contra, taught me how to, he said all the way to let your drum down unless the weather gets too tight. But he said when you're tight, keep it up all the time. Don't let it down, because no matter what you do you can get it back in the same place again. So that's why my drums sound so good. And so far everybody that came out of the club, I would play…

That's right, that's right. When did you start using the hi-hat or sock cymbal, what do you call that hi-hat or sock cymbal? That's a hi-hat cymbal. I thought well I got modern just like everybody else did, you know.

items.title: Minor "Ram" Hall Interview, 1958-09-02
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Of the New Orleans drummers, do you remember any of the early ones like old man Contrell or Contrell? [INTERVIEWEE] Yeah, yeah.

ctx.x: Yeah. Any other drummers you can remember there? Ever hear of Walter Brundy? Yeah, sure. How was he? He was a good drummer.

See, another day that I remember, Walter Brundy and the Zeno, while old man Contrell and now let's see, I can remember. Old timers. No, that's... Remember Mac Murray? No, I don't, no. I've heard of him, but I don't remember him.
